Lateral patellar dislocation results in bone contusion at the medial patella and along the lateral aspect of the lateral femoral condyle. The patellar usually relocates, and the typical bone contusions are the key MRI features to diagnose transient lateral patellar dislocation (Fig. 7). in_text_mentions: rgency department following a motorcycle collision with severe left knee pain. On physical examination, the left knee was locked in full extension. The patella was in internal vertical rotation (Fig. 1A), tender to palpation, and restricted in mobility. The knee joint showed mild effusion, and distal neurovascular examination was intact. The patient had no prior history of patellar instability or patellar dislocation. Figure 1.Case 1: Clinical appearance of the knee (A), radiographs (B), and 3D CT reconstructions (C) demonstrating a locked, lateral, 70° vertically rotated, intra-articular pate

Radiographs revealed a laterally displaced patella with vertical rotation and mild patellofemoral osteoarthritic changes, including patellar osteophytes (Fig. 1B). A skyline view could not be obtained because of severe pain. Initial attempts at closed reduction in the emergency department using an intra-articular local anesthetic were unsuccessful.

As plain radiographs did not define the cause of irreducibility, a computed tomography (CT) scan was obtained before any further intervention. CT demonstrated a locked patellar rotation of approximately 70°, with the articular surface facing laterally, and identified a definite osteophyte (4.7 × 4.3 mm) at the inferomedial pole of the patella that was impacted against the lateral edge of the medial femoral condyle. No osteochondral fractures were identified (Fig. 1C).

Attempts were made for telehealth follow-up. Unfortunately, these were unsuccessful, and no follow-up information was available.

in_text_mentions: Long leg standing radiographs showed severe lateral OA, a femorotibial angle (FTA) of 160°, and a hip-knee-ankle angle (HKA) of valgus 12°. Skyline view radiographs showed the patella was dislocated to the lateral side of the lateral femoral condyle, the central ridge was absent, and the trochlear groove was hypoplastic (sulcus angle was 169°) (Figures 1(a)–1(d)). Computed tomography (CT) scan showed that the tibial tubercle-trochlear groove distance was 22 mm, and the surgical epicondylar axis (SEA) was rotated 7.6° externally from the posterior condylar axis (PCA) (Figure 1(e)).

in_text_mentions: MRI of the left knee was performed 1 month prior to her initial visit to our clinic (Figure 2). This study revealed a laterally dislocated patella with disruption of the MPFL ligament and medial retinaculum with an associated bony avulsion fracture. The femoral trochlea was noted to be dysplastic with edema and cartilage loss localized at the lateral trochlea. Her TT-TG distance was significantly elevated at 26.4 mm. Other structures of the knee appeared to be intact.
